text:
Aims for Using Walking Aids?
• Increase area of Base of support (BOS)
• Better BALANCE – maintain the centre of gravity (CG) over BOS
• Redistribute weight bearing area with decreased loading on injured part
• Improve proprioception
• Decrease pain
• Assist weak muscles
→ Improve stability and independency

text:
Selection of Walking Aids
Physiotherapist considers patient’s
• Disability level
• Stability
• Muscles strength of both upper & lower limb
• Coordination of upper & lower limb
• Weight bearing status
• Non-weight bearing (NWB)
• Touch down (TDW)
• Partial weight bearing (PWB)
• Weight bear as tolerated (WBAT)
• Full weight bearing (FWB)
• Patient’s ability to manipulate the walking aids (both cognitive & physical status)

text:
Walking Frame
Rollator
• Maximum stability and widest base of support
• Rollator (two/four wheels)- allow patient to gently push for moving forward.
• Frame: lift up & placed forward BEFORE step out
• Foldable design for easier transportation & storage
• Sequence: Frame → bad leg → good leg

text:
Limitations of Walking Frame/Rollator
➢ Relatively difficult to store and transport
➢ NOT RECOMMENDED for stairs walking
➢ Slower gait speed (Rollator FASTER than frame)

text:
Axillary Crutches
• Patients who require LESS support with better stability or support compared with walking frame/ rollator
• allow more flexible gait patterns with faster pace
• Fitting x 2: height of the crutches AND level of hand piece
• Sequence depends on gait pattern

text:
Limitations for Axillary crutches
➢ Less stable as less support than walking frame/rollator
➢ Improper use may cause injury to the neurovascular structures at the axillary region
➢ Require good standing balance from patient
➢ NOT recommended for Elderly/ Geriatrics
➢ Insufficient upper limb & trunk stability & reduced coordination

➢ Require good standing balance & upper-body strength as well as coordination
➢ Geriatric patient sometimes feel insecure with these crutches (NOT recommended for Elderly)

text:
Quadripod
• Good ability of individuals pretty good balance & stability
• ONLY for Full weight bearing (FWB)
• Place at GOOD/ UNAFFECTED side
• Easy to use for stairs walking & other confined areas
• Easy storage & usage
• Bigger base = more support
• Sequence:
• Modified 4pt: Quad → weak leg
→ good leg
• Modified 2pt: (Quad + weak leg)
→ good leg

Limitations for Quadripod
• Provided limited support & weaker stability as small base of support
• NOT for other weight bearing status (like Non weight bear & partial weight bearing) EXCEPT Full Weight Bearing

text:
Three-point gait pattern (3pt gait)
➢ Bilateral crutches or walker
➢ Used in NWB only
➢ Good side: FWB; Affected NWB
➢ At least 50% of body weight is transmitted through the upper limb.
• UL strength, core stability & good lower limb must be assessed BEFORE attempting this gait pattern
➢ The energy cost is about TWICE as normal walking (more tiring)

text:
Modified 3pt gait pattern
➢ Requires two crutches or a walker Touch down weight bearing (TDWB)
➢ Good side FWB + Affected side Touch Down Partial weight bearing (PWB)
➢ Good side FWB + Affected side > 50% BW Sequence: Crutches → good leg

text:
Four-point gait pattern (4pt gait)
• A four-point gait pattern is used when the patient requires maximum assistance with balance.
• Requires use of bilateral walking aids ie. pair of crutches/sticks
• Sequence:
• Rt Crutch → Lt Foot → Lt crutch → Rt Foot
• A slower gait pattern, but a stable one.
source_file: 17 - 5. Mobility Walking Aids 助行工具.pdf

text:
Two-point gait pattern (2pt gait)
➢ Require use of bilateral walking aids
➢ Faster pace than four-point gait but less stable
➢ Nearly as NORMAL gait pattern & be encouraged
➢ Require ability on co-ordination between moving walking aid together with the contralateral lower limb
➢ Sequence:
➢ (Rt Crutch + Lt Foot)→ (Lt crutch + Rt Foot )

Stairs with Crutches
➢ Non-weight bearing
➢ With rails
➢ Good side hand on rail, crutches on other hand
➢ Upstairs: Good leg → Crutches + bad leg
➢ Down stairs: Crutches + bad leg → good leg
➢ No rails
➢ Up-stairs: Good leg → Crutches + bad leg
➢ Down stairs: Crutches + bad leg → good leg
